Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 31, verse 1–2:

(p-710) Surat Luqman is Meccan, and it has either thirty-three or thirty-four verses.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Alif, Lam, Mim.﴾ ﴿These are the verses of the Wise Book.﴾ [The word "Hakim" (wise) is] in the sense of "possessing wisdom" (dhi al-hikmah), or it is described with an attribute of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, by way of metaphorical attribution (al-isnad al-majazi).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 31, verse 1–2:

(p-710) Surat Luqman is Meccan, and it has either thirty-three or thirty-four verses.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Alif, Lam, Mim.﴾ ﴿These are the verses of the Wise Book.﴾ [The word "Hakim" (wise) is] in the sense of "possessing wisdom" (dhi al-hikmah), or it is described with an attribute of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, by way of metaphorical attribution (al-isnad al-majazi).

Hudan wa rahmatan (هُدًى ورَحْمَةً) are two circumstantial accusatives (ḥālān) referring to "the verses" (al-āyāt). The governing element (al-ʿāmil) is the meaning of the demonstrative in "tilka" (those). Ḥamzah reads it in the nominative (bil-rafʿ), on the basis that "tilka" is the subject (mubtadaʾ), "āyātu al-Kitāb" (the verses of the Book) is its predicate (khabar), and "hudan" is a second predicate after the first, or the predicate of an omitted subject (mubtada' maḥdhūf), meaning: "huwa" (it is), or "hiya hudan wa raḥmatun" (it is guidance and mercy). ﴿Lil-muḥsinīn﴾ (for the doers of good) refers to those who perform the good deeds mentioned in His saying (in the verse that follows).

﴿Those who establish the prayer, and give the zakat, and are certain of the Hereafter.﴾ Its parallel is the verse of Aws:

> The shrewd man who guesses about you as if he had seen and heard.

Or [the meaning is]: for those who do all that is good, then He singled out from among them those who maintain these three, for their excellence. (p-٧١١)

﴿Those are upon guidance﴾ is a mubtada' (subject) and khabar (predicate). ﴿from their Lord﴾ is a ṣifah (qualifier) of هُدًى (hudan, "guidance"). ﴿And those are the successful﴾ is an ʿaṭf (conjunction) upon it.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 31, verse 6:

﴿And among people is he who purchases idle talk﴾ It was revealed concerning al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, who used to buy the reports of the Kisras (the Persian kings) from Persia, and he would say: "Muhammad recounts a portion of the story of ʿAd and Thamud, but I will tell you the tales of the Kisras." So people would incline to his talk and abandon listening to the Qur'an. Idle talk (al-lahw) is every falsehood that diverts one from what is good and from what is of concern. Idle talk includes such things as evening chatter about fables that have no basis, and singing (al-ghina'). Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, used to swear that it refers to singing. It has been said: singing corrupts the heart, wastes wealth, and provokes the anger of the Lord. And from the Prophet (ﷺ): "No man raises his voice in singing except that Allah sends upon him two devils, one on this shoulder and the other on that shoulder, and they keep striking him with their feet until he is the one who stops."

The word *ishtira'* (purchases) is from *shira'* (buying), as is narrated concerning al-Nadr; or it is from the phrase "they purchased disbelief in exchange for faith" (﴿اشْتَرَوُا الكُفْرَ بِالإيمانِ﴾), meaning they substituted it for it and chose it over it, i.e., they prefer the talk of falsehood over the talk of truth. The attribution of *lahw* (idle talk) to *hadith* (talk) is for explanation, in the sense of *min* (from), because idle talk may come from talk or from other than talk, so it is specified as talk. The intended meaning of *hadith* here is reprehensible talk, as in the hadith: "Talk in the mosque devours good deeds as an animal devours grass." Alternatively, it is for partition (*tab'id*), as if it were said: "And among people is he who purchases some of the talk which is idle talk." 

﴿to mislead﴾ i.e., to turn people away from entering Islam and from listening to the Qur'an. *Liyudilla* (to mislead) is read by Makki and Abu ʿAmr, meaning that he remains steadfast in the misguidance he was upon and increases in it. ﴿from the way of Allah﴾ i.e., from the religion of Islam and the Qur'an. ﴿without knowledge﴾ i.e., in ignorance of the burden of sin he bears by it. ﴿and take it﴾ i.e., the way, with the accusative (*wa-yattakhidha*) read by Kufans other than Abu Bakr, being conjoined to *liyudilla*; whoever reads it in the nominative conjoins it to *yashtari*. ﴿in mockery﴾ read with a sukun on the zay and the hamza by Hamza, and with a damma on the zay without hamza by Hafs, and others read it with a damma on the zay and the hamza. ﴿For them is a humiliating punishment﴾ i.e., it humiliates them. The word *man* (he who), because of its generality, applies to the singular and the plural, i.e., al-Nadr and those like him.

﴿When Our verses are recited to him, he turns away in arrogance﴾ He turns away from reflecting upon them, puffed up with pride and raising himself above listening to the Qur'an.

﴿as though he had not heard them﴾ His state in this resembles the state of one who did not hear them. It is a ḥāl (circumstantial clause) relating to *mustakbiran* (in arrogance). The original form is *ka-annahu* (as though he), and the pronoun is a *ḍamīr al-sha'n* (pronoun of the matter).

﴿as though there were in his ears a* waqr* (heaviness)﴾ *Waqr* means heaviness, and it is a ḥāl relating to *lam yasma'hā* (he had not heard them). The word *"udhnayhi"* (his two ears) is read by Nafi'.

﴿So give him tidings of a painful punishment.﴾
﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds, for them are the Gardens of Bliss﴾ There is no waqf (pause for stopping) at it, because.

Verse 9 of Surah 31 (Luqman), with al-Nasafi's commentary:

﴿Abiding therein forever.﴾ This is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) referring back to the pronoun in "for them." ﴿The promise of God, in truth.﴾ Both are verbal nouns (maṣdarān) used for emphasis (mu'akkidān). The first is emphatic of itself (mu'akkid li-nafsihi), and the second is emphatic of something other than itself (mu'akkid li-ghayrihi), since "for them are the Gardens of Bliss" means "God has promised them the Gardens of Bliss." Thus the meaning of promise is emphasized by a promise, and "ḥaqqan" (in truth) indicates the meaning of firmness (al-thubūt), so the meaning of promise is emphasized by it. The object of emphasis for both is ﴿for them are the Gardens of Bliss﴾ [Luqman: 8]. ﴿And He is the Almighty﴾, the One whom nothing overpowers, so He humiliates His enemies with a humiliating punishment. ﴿The All-Wise﴾, in what He does, so He rewards His friends with lasting bliss.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 31, verse 10:

﴿He created the heavens without pillars﴾ — ʿamad is the plural of ʿimad (pillar). ﴿that you see﴾ — the pronoun refers to the heavens, and it is a testimony to their seeing them as having no pillars, in response to His words "without pillars," just as you say to your companion, "Here I am without sword or spear, you see me." It has no place in i'rab (grammatical case), because it is either a new, independent clause, or it is in the genitive position as an attribute of ʿamad, meaning: without pillars that are seen. That is, He supported them with a pillar that is not seen, which is His holding them up by His power. ﴿And He cast into the earth firm mountains﴾ — mountains that are fixed, ﴿lest it shake with you﴾ — so that it would not quake with you. ﴿And He spread throughout it﴾ — and dispersed and scattered in it ﴿every kind of moving creature.﴾ ﴿And We sent down water from the sky, and made grow in it every noble pair﴾ — every kind, ﴿noble﴾ — good.

This is a demonstrative referring to what was mentioned of His creatures, "this is the creation of Allah" meaning His creation (makhluq). "Then show me what those besides Him have created" — meaning their gods (ālihatahum). He rebuked them by pointing out that these great things are among what Allah created: "show me what your gods have created, so that they deserve worship from you." "Rather, the wrongdoers are in manifest error": He turned away from rebuking them to affirming upon them that they are immersed in an error beyond which there is no error.

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (*Madarik al-Tanzil*) on surah 31, verse 12:**

﴿We certainly gave Luqman wisdom﴾. He is Luqman son of Ba'ura' (Bāʿūrāʾ), the son of Ayyub's sister or the son of his maternal aunt. It is also said that he was among the descendants of Azar. He lived a thousand years and met Dawud, peace be upon him, and took knowledge from him. He used to give legal rulings (*yuftī*) before the mission of Dawud, peace be upon him. When Dawud was sent as a prophet, he stopped issuing rulings. He was asked about this and said: "Shall I not be content when I have been made sufficient?" It is also said that he was a tailor, a carpenter, or a shepherd. It is also said that he was a judge among the Children of Israel. Ikrima and al-Sha'bi said he was a prophet, but the majority hold that he was a sage (*ḥakīm*) and was not a prophet. It is also said that he was given the choice between prophethood and wisdom (*ḥikmah*) and chose wisdom, which is correctness in speech and action. It is also said that he was a student of a thousand prophets, and a thousand prophets were students of him.

The *an* in ﴿أنِ اشْكُرْ لِلَّهِ﴾ (*an*) is explanatory (*mufassira*), and the meaning is: "that is, give thanks to God," because the giving of wisdom carries the sense of saying. God, exalted is He, has drawn attention to the fact that the original wisdom and the true knowledge are acting upon them both, worshipping God, and giving thanks to Him, since He explained the giving of wisdom as an exhortation to give thanks. It is also said that a man is not wise until he is wise in his speech, his deeds, his companionship, and his association with others.

Al-Sari al-Saqati said: "Gratitude is that you do not disobey God with His blessings." Al-Junayd said: "It is that you do not see any partner with Him in His blessings." It is also said that it is the acknowledgment of incapacity to give thanks. The summary is that the gratitude of the heart is recognition, the gratitude of the tongue is praise, and the gratitude of the limbs is obedience, and seeing one's incapacity in all of these is a sign that all of them are accepted.

﴿And whoever gives thanks, he gives thanks only for his own self﴾, because its benefit returns to him, for he seeks increase. ﴿And whoever is ungrateful﴾ for the blessing, ﴿then God is Self-Sufficient﴾, not in need of thanks, ﴿Praiseworthy﴾, deserving to be praised even if no one praises Him.

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 31, verse 13:**

﴿And when﴾: that is, remember when ﴿Luqman said to his son﴾, (Anʿam or Ashkam, a variant reading of the name of the son), ﴿while he was admonishing him: "O my son﴾ (with the sukun, read by Makki), ﴿"O my son"﴾ (with the fatha, read by Hafs throughout the Qur'an), ﴿do not associate partners with Allah. Indeed, association is a tremendous wrong﴾, because it equates between one who has no blessing except that it comes from Him and one who has no blessing at all.

﴿And We have enjoined upon man (concerning) his parents. His mother carried him in weakness upon weakness﴾: that is, she carried him, growing weaker and weaker, that is, her weakness increased upon weakness, that is, her frailty grew and multiplied, because the more the pregnancy continued or grew, the heavier and weaker she became. ﴿And his weaning is in two years﴾: that is, his being weaned from breastfeeding at the completion of two years. ﴿Give thanks to Me and to your parents﴾: this explains "We have enjoined," that is, We enjoined him to give thanks to Us and to his parents. And His saying ﴿His mother carried him in weakness upon weakness and his weaning is in two years﴾ is a parenthetical clause (i'tiraḍ) between the explained and the explainer (al-mufassar wa-l-mufassir). This is because, when He enjoined (kindness to) the parents, He mentioned what the mother endures and suffers of hardships in carrying him and weaning him over this long period, as a reminder of her great right, singled out for mention. And it is related from Ibn 'Uyayna: whoever prays the five prayers has indeed given thanks to God, and whoever supplicates for his parents after the five prayers has indeed given thanks to them both. ﴿To Me is the (final) return﴾: that is, your return is to Me, and your reckoning is upon Me. (p-715)

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 31, verse 15:

﴿And if they strive with you to make you associate with Me that of which you have no knowledge, do not obey them.﴾ By negating knowledge of it, he intends negating it itself, i.e., "Do not associate with Me that which is not a thing," meaning the idols. ﴿So do not obey them﴾ in associating partners (with Me). ﴿And keep them company in this world with kindness﴾: "kindness" (ma'ruf) is an adjective of a verbal noun that has been omitted, i.e., "companionship of kindness," good, with good character, forbearance, tolerance, righteousness and maintaining family ties. ﴿And follow the way of those who turn to Me in repentance﴾, i.e., the way of the believers in your religion, and do not follow their way in it, even though you are commanded to treat them well in this world. Ibn 'Ata' said: "Keep company with the one in whom you see the lights of My service." ﴿Then to Me is your return﴾, i.e., your return and their return. ﴿So I will inform you of what you used to do﴾, meaning I will reward you for your faith and I will reward them for their disbelief. These two verses have been inserted parenthetically by way of digression, as an emphasis on the prohibition of associating partners that is in Luqman's counsel. That is to say: We enjoined upon him (to honour) his parents and commanded him not to obey them in associating partners, even if they strive with all their striving, because of its ugliness.

"O my son, indeed it (the deed), if it be the weight of a grain of mustard seed," (read with the nominative) is the reading of Madani (Nafi'), and the pronoun refers to the matter (al-qissa, "the story/affair"). He made "al-mithqal" feminine because it is in construct with "al-habba" (the grain), as in the verse of the poet:

"Just as the chest of the spear was stained with blood."

Here "kana" is complete (tamma, not requiring a predicate). The rest of the readers read it with the accusative (naṣb), and the pronoun refers to the state (al-hay'a) of the deed, good or bad. That is: if it is, in smallness, like the grain of mustard seed, ﴿then it will be in a rock, or in the heavens, or in the earth﴾, meaning: then, despite its smallness, it would be in the most hidden and most secure place, like the inside of a rock (p-716) or wherever it is, in the upper world or the lower world. Most (scholars) hold that the rock is the one upon which the earth rests, and it is Sijjin, in which the deeds of the wicked are recorded, and it is not part of the earth. ﴿Allah will bring it forth﴾ on the Day of Resurrection, and He will call its doer to account for it. ﴿Indeed Allah is Subtle﴾ by the reaching of His knowledge to every hidden thing, ﴿Aware﴾, knowing its essence; or "Subtle" in bringing it out, "Aware" of its resting place.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 31, verse 17:

﴿O my dear son, establish the prayer, enjoin what is right, forbid what is wrong, and bear patiently whatever befalls you﴾ — (bear patiently) for the sake of Allah, Exalted is He, when you enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong, or (bear patiently) what befalls you of trials, for they bring about gifts (al-minah). ﴿Indeed, that﴾ — what I have enjoined upon you — ﴿is of the firm resolve of matters﴾. That is, of what Allah has resolved (ʿazama) of matters, i.e., decreed with a decree of obligation and binding, meaning He commanded it as an absolute command. It is an instance of naming the object by the verbal noun (tasmiyat al-maf'ul bi'l-masdar), and its origin is from "maʿzumat al-umur" (the resolved matters), i.e., those that are decided and obligatory. This is evidence that these acts of worship were commanded in all the nations.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 31, verse 18:

﴿And do not turn your cheek away from people﴾, i.e., do not turn away from them out of arrogance. "Tusā'ir" (تُصاعِرْ) is read by Abu 'Amr, Nafi', Hamzah and 'Ali, and it has the same meaning as "tusa''ir" (تُصَعِّرُ). Al-sa'r (الصَعْر) is a disease that afflicts the camel, causing it to twist its neck. The meaning is: turn towards people with your face in humility, and do not turn to them the side of your face and its profile as the arrogant do. ﴿And do not walk upon the earth exultantly﴾, i.e., do not strut about with exultation, or the verbal noun (maṣdar) is placed in the position of the circumstantial accusative (ḥāl), meaning: exultant; or: do not walk for the sake of exultation and insolence. ﴿Indeed, Allah does not love everyone self-deluded﴾, arrogant, ﴿boastful﴾, one who counts his virtues out of haughtiness.

The Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 31, verse 19:

﴿And be moderate﴾. Al-qasd (moderation) is the middle course between excessive haste and slackness, ﴿in your walking﴾. That is, walk with a pace that is between two paces: do not trudge like one who feigns lifelessness, nor leap like the rogues (al-shutṭār). The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Haste in walking takes away the radiance (bahā') of the believer (p-٧١٧)." As for the saying of ʿĀʾisha concerning ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, that "when he walked, he hastened," she meant a brisk pace, distinct from the trudging of one feigning lifelessness. And from Ibn Masʿūd, may Allah be pleased with him: "They were forbidden from the khabab (a bounding gait) of the Jews and the dabīb (a slow, plodding gait) of the Christians, but rather (walk) with a pace between these two." It was also said that its meaning is: look to the place of your feet, being humble.

﴿And lower your voice﴾, that is, reduce it and temper it, ﴿indeed, the most hateful of voices﴾, that is, the most fearsome of them, ﴿is the braying of donkeys﴾. This is because its beginning is a zafīr (exhalation) and its end is a shahīq (inhalation), like the sound of the people of the Fire. And from al-Thawrī: "Every creature's cry is tasbīḥ (glorification), except the donkey, for it brays upon seeing the devil." For this reason Allah called it "munkar" (hateful). In likening those who raise their voices to donkeys, and in depicting their voices as braying, there is an admonition that raising the voice is in the extreme of disliked conduct. This is supported by what is related: "The Prophet (ﷺ) liked that a man be soft-voiced and disliked that he be loud-voiced."

He used the singular "the braying of donkeys" and did not use the plural, because He did not intend to mention the voice of each individual member of this species so as to make it plural; rather, the intent is that every species of animal has a voice, and the most hateful of the voices of these species is the voice of this species, so it is right that it be stated in the singular.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 31, verse 20:

﴿Have you not seen that Allah has subjected to you whatever is in the heavens﴾ meaning: the sun, the moon, the stars, the clouds and other things; ﴿and whatever is on the earth﴾ meaning: the seas, the rivers, the minerals, the animals and other things; ﴿and has completed for you His favours﴾ and perfected them; ﴿His blessings﴾ — Madani, Abu 'Amr, Sahl and Hafs read "ni'mah" (in the singular) and others read "ni'mat" (in the plural). A ni'mah (blessing) is every benefit intended as a kindness; ﴿apparent﴾ through observation, ﴿and hidden﴾ — that which is not known except through proof. Then it has been said: the apparent are sight, hearing, tongue and the rest of the outward limbs, and the hidden are the heart, the intellect, understanding and what is similar to these. It is related in the supplication of Musa (peace be upon him): "My Lord, guide me to the most hidden of Your blessings upon Your servants," and He said: "The most hidden of My blessings upon them is the breath." It has also been said: lightening of the laws (sharia'), reducing the means of wrongdoing (dhara'i'), creation and character (khuluq), attaining gifts, averting calamities, acceptance among people, and the pleasure of the Lord. Ibn 'Abbas said: the apparent is what He has made proportionate of your creation, and the hidden is what He has concealed of your faults. ﴿And among the people is one who argues about Allah without knowledge, guidance or an illuminating Book﴾ — it was revealed concerning al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, and it has passed in the chapter on Hajj.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 31, verse 21:

﴿And when it is said to them, "Follow what Allah has sent down," they say, "Rather, we follow that which we found our fathers upon." Even if the Shaytan (Satan) were calling them to the punishment of the blazing Fire?﴾ Its meaning: "Would they follow them even if the Shaytan were calling them, that is, while the Shaytan is calling them to the punishment?"

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 31, verse 22:

﴿And whoever submits his face to Allah﴾. It is governed here by "ilā" (to), whereas in ﴿Yes, whoever submits his face to Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 112] it is governed by "li" (for). With "li" its meaning is that he made his face, which is his very self and essence, sound (sālim) for Allah, that is, sincere (khāliṣ) to Him. With "ilā" its meaning is that he handed over his self to Him, just as one hands over goods to a man when they are delivered to him, and the intended sense is reliance upon Him (tawakkul) and entrusting of the matter to Him. ﴿And he is a doer of good (muḥsin)﴾ in what he does. ﴿Then he has grasped﴾ meaning he has held fast and clung ﴿to the handhold (al-ʿurwa)﴾, which is that by which a thing is suspended, ﴿the most firm (al-wuthqā)﴾, being the feminine of al-awthaq. He depicted the state of the one who relies upon Allah by the state of one who wished to lower himself from a high cliff and took precaution for himself by grasping the strongest handhold of a sturdy rope whose breaking is trusted to be impossible. ﴿And to Allah belongs the outcome of all matters﴾, that is, they all return to Him, and He will recompense for them.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 31, verse 23:

﴿And whoever disbelieves﴾ and does not submit his face to Allah. ﴿So let not his disbelief grieve you﴾: from ḥazana (to grieve). Nāfiʿ reads "yuḥzinka" from aḥzana (to cause grief), meaning: let not the disbelief of those who disbelieve concern you. ﴿To Us is their return, and We will inform them of what they did﴾: We will punish them for their deeds. ﴿Indeed, Allah is Knowing of what is within the breasts﴾: Indeed, Allah knows what is in the hearts of His servants, and so He deals with them according to that.

﴿We let them enjoy [worldly life] for a little while﴾ with their worldly goods, ﴿then We will drive them﴾, i.e., compel them, ﴿to a harsh punishment﴾, i.e., a severe one. He likened the compulsion of their being tormented and the burden of it upon them to the compulsion of one who is forced (al-mudtarr) to something (p-719). "Harshness" (al-ghilẓ) is used metaphorically from solid, thick bodies (ajram al-ghalīẓa), and what is meant is severity and weight upon the one being punished.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 31, verse 25:

﴿And if you ask them, "Who created the heavens and the earth?" they will surely say, "Allah." Say, "Praise be to Allah."﴾ This is a binding argument against them, based on their acknowledgment that the One who created the heavens and the earth is Allah alone, and that therefore all praise and thanks are due to Him alone, and that none other should be worshipped along with Him. Then He said, ﴿Rather, most of them do not know﴾, meaning that this (conclusion) is binding upon them, but when they are alerted to it, they do not pay heed.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 31, verse 26:

﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth. Indeed, Allah is the Free of need﴾ from the praise of those who praise [Him], ﴿the Praiseworthy﴾, the One deserving of praise even if they do not praise Him.

The disbelievers said: "Indeed this" — that is, the revelation — "is speech that will come to an end." So God made known that His speech does not come to an end, by His saying:

﴿And if whatever trees are in the earth were pens, and the sea, with seven more seas to replenish it, were ink, the words of God would not be exhausted.﴾

"And the sea" (al-baḥra) in the accusative is read by Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub, coordinating it with the noun of inna, which is "mā" (the pronoun in mā), while the nominative reading is according to the position (maḥall) of inna and its operand. That is: if it were established that the trees are pens, and the sea was established as extended by seven seas. Or it is in the nominative by way of the inceptive (ibtida'), and the wa' is for the circumstantial (ḥal), meaning: even if the trees were pens while the sea was extended.

It was also read "yumiddu-hu" (with the verb). The expected form of the sentence would have been: "And if the trees were pens and the sea were ink," but the mention of ink was dispensed with by his saying "yamuddu-hu," because it derives from your saying "madda al-dawāta" and "amaddahā" (he supplied the inkwell). He made the greatest sea like the inkwell, and made the seven seas filled with ink, so they continually pour their ink into it without interruption. The meaning is: even if the trees of the earth were pens, and the sea were extended by seven seas, and with those pens and that ink the words of God were written, the words of God would not be exhausted, and the pens and ink would be spent, as in His saying:

﴿Say: If the sea were ink for the words of my Lord, the sea would be spent before the words of my Lord are exhausted.﴾ [al-Kahf: 109]

If you say: you claimed that His saying "and the sea extends it" is a circumstantial clause in one of the two nominative readings, and there is no pronoun in it referring back to the one it qualifies (dhū al-ḥāl). I say: it is like your saying "I came while the army was lined up," and similar circumstances whose ruling is that of adverbs of time and place.

He mentioned "a tree" in the singular because the intent is to detail the trees, tracing them tree by tree, until no species of tree and no single tree remains that has not been cut into pens. "Kalimāt" (words), which is the plural of paucity, was preferred over "kalim," which is the plural of abundance, because its meaning is: the seas cannot suffice to write His words, so how could they suffice for His words?! "Indeed God is Mighty" — nothing can overpower Him; "Wise" — nothing escapes His knowledge and wisdom, so His words and His wisdoms are never exhausted.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 31, verse 28:

﴿Your creation and your resurrection are not but as [the creation and resurrection of] a single soul.﴾ It means: except as the creation of a single soul and the resurrection of a single soul, and the second part has been omitted because it is understood. That is, with respect to His power, the few and the many are equal, so no matter of affairs occupies Him from another. ﴿Indeed, Allah is All-Hearing﴾ of the words of the polytheists who say there is no resurrection, ﴿All-Seeing﴾ of their deeds, so He will recompense them.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 31, verse 29:

﴿Have you not seen that Allah causes the night to enter into the day﴾ He makes the darkness of the night enter into the light of the day when the night approaches. ﴿And causes the day to enter into the night, and has subjected the sun and the moon﴾ for the benefit of His servants. ﴿Each﴾ i.e., each one of the sun and the moon ﴿runs﴾ in its orbit and traverses it ﴿for a term specified﴾ until the Day of Resurrection, or until a known time: the sun until the end of the year, and the moon until the end of the month. ﴿And Allah is All-Aware of what you do﴾ — with the yā' (reading "ya'malūna," "they do," with the third person), it is read by ʿAyyāsh as well.

It also indicates, through the alternation of night and day, their increase and decrease, and the running of the two luminaries in their orbits, a precise measure and reckoning, and through His encompassing knowledge of all the deeds of creation, the immensity of His power and the perfection of His wisdom.

That is because Allah is the Truth, and because what they call upon besides Him is falsehood, and because Allah is the Most High, the Great. The reading of ﴿وأنَّ ما يَدْعُونَ﴾ with the letter ya (i.e., "yad'una" with ya) is that of the Iraqi readers other than Abu Bakr, meaning ﴿مِن دُونِهِ الباطِلُ﴾ ... [as the verse reads].

Meaning: That attribute which He has been described with, from the wonders of His power and His wisdom, which living, powerful, knowing beings are unable to achieve, so how about the inanimate object that they call upon besides Allah?! It is only because of the fact that He is the Truth, the established divinity, and that whatever is besides Him is the falsehood of divinity, and that He is the Most High in rank, the Great in authority.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 31, verse 31:

(p-721) ﴿Have you not seen that the ship﴾ is also read "al-Fulk" (الفُلُكَ). Every pattern of the form fu'l (فُعْلٌ) may take the form fu'ul (فُعُلٌ), just as every fu'ul may take the form fu'l. ﴿runs upon the sea by the favour of God﴾, that is, by His kindness and mercy, or by the wind, since the wind is among the favours of God. ﴿That He may show you of His signs﴾, that is, the wonders of His power at sea when you ride it. ﴿Indeed in that are signs for every steadfast one﴾ in the face of His trials, ﴿grateful﴾ for His blessings. These two are the attributes of the believer, for faith is two halves: half of it is gratitude and half of it is patience. So it is as if He said: indeed in that are signs for every believer.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 31, verse 32:

﴿And when a wave covers them like shadows﴾ i.e., the disbelievers, ﴿a wave like shadows﴾. The wave rises and then returns like shadows, and the ẓullah (shadow, canopy) is everything that shades you, whether a mountain, a cloud, or other things. ﴿They call upon God, sincere to Him in religion. But when He delivers them to the land, some of them are moderate.﴾ That is: they remain upon the faith and sincerity they had, and do not return to disbelief; or he is moderate (muqtaṣid, i.e., middling) in disbelief and wrongdoing, having been restrained to some degree, and does not go to extremes in his disbelief; or he is moderate in the sincerity he had at sea. The meaning is that this sincerity that arises at the time of fear does not remain in anyone at all, and the muqtaṣid is rare and scarce. ﴿And none deny Our signs﴾ i.e., their reality, ﴿except every treacherous ungrateful one﴾, a betrayer, and khatr (treachery) is the worst kind of betrayal, ﴿ungrateful﴾ toward his Lord.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 31, verse 33:

﴿O humankind, fear your Lord and dread a Day when no parent will avail anything on behalf of their child﴾ lā yaqḍī ʿanhu shay'an (does not discharge anything on his behalf). The meaning is: "does not avail in it," and the preposition was elided. ﴿Nor will a child avail anything on behalf of their parent﴾ (huwa jāzin ʿan wālidihi shay'an) comes in a form of emphasis that the preceding clause does not have, because the nominal sentence (al-jumla al-ismiyya) is more emphatic than the verbal sentence (al-jumla al-fiʿliyya). To this is added his saying "huwa" and his saying "mawlūd." The reason for this is that the address is to the believers, and some of them had parents who died in disbelief. So it was intended to cut off their hopes that they might benefit their parents through intercession (shafāʿa) in the Hereafter. The emphasis in the word "mawlūd" is that if one of them interceded for his nearest father, from whom he was born, his intercession would not be accepted, let alone that he should intercede for his grandfathers. This is because "walad" applies to a son and a son's son, whereas "mawlūd" applies to whoever has been born from you. Thus it is in al-Kashshaf.

﴿Indeed, the promise of God﴾ regarding the resurrection, the reckoning, and the recompense ﴿is true. So do not let the worldly life deceive you﴾ with its adornments, for its bounty is near and its pleasure is transient. ﴿And do not let the Deceiver deceive you about God﴾: the Shaytan, or the world, or false hope.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 31, verse 34:

﴿Indeed, Allah has with Him the knowledge of the Hour﴾, that is, the time of its establishment. ﴿And He sends down﴾ (with the doubled letter, *tashdid*, read by Ibn ʿĀmir of Damascus, Madinan, and ʿAsim; it is a conjunction, *ʿatf*, upon what the adverbial phrase (*zarf*, an adverb of time or place) implies of the verb; its implied sense is: "Indeed Allah possesses the knowledge of the Hour, and He sends down") ﴿the rain﴾ at its appointed time (*ibban*), without advance or delay. ﴿And He knows what is in the wombs﴾: whether it is male or female, and whether it is complete or deficient? ﴿And no soul knows﴾ whether it is pious or wicked ﴿what it will earn tomorrow﴾ of good or evil. It may be that a person intends good and then does evil, or intends evil and then does good. ﴿And no soul knows in what land it will die﴾, that is, where it will die. It may be that a person settles in a land, drives its tent pegs, and says, "I will never leave it," and then fate casts it to distant places, and it dies in a place it never imagined.

It is reported that the Angel of Death passed by Sulayman (peace be upon him) and began looking at one of his companions. The man asked, "Who is this?" He was told, "The Angel of Death." The man said, "It seems he wants me." He asked Sulayman, peace be upon him, to carry him on the wind and set him down in the lands of India, and he did so. Then the Angel of Death said to Sulayman, "My continued gazing at him was out of wonder, for I was commanded to seize his soul in India, and he was with you." Knowledge (*ʿilm*) belongs to Allah, while *dirayah* (knowing through one's own effort and reasoning) belongs to the servants, because *dirayah* carries the meaning of cunning and stratagem. The meaning is: a soul does not know what is specific to it, even if it employs its stratagems. Nothing is more specific to a person than his earning and his final end. If there is no way for him to know these two, then knowledge of anything else is even more remote.

As for the astrologer who foretells the time of rain or death, he speaks by analogy and reasoning from the rising stars. What is attained through evidence is not unseen, although it is merely conjecture (*zann*), and conjecture is not knowledge.

It is reported from the Prophet (ﷺ): "The keys of the unseen are five," and he recited this verse. It is also reported from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that whoever claims knowledge of these five has lied.

Al-Mansur saw in his dream the form of the Angel of Death, and asked him about the length of his life. He pointed with his five fingers, and the interpreters of dreams interpreted this as five years, five months, and five days. Abu Hanifa, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "It is an allusion to this verse, for these five matters none knows except Allah." ﴿Indeed Allah is Knowing﴾ of the unseen ﴿and Aware﴾ of what has happened and what will happen.

It is reported from al-Zuhri, may Allah be pleased with him: "Recite much of Surah Luqman, for in it are wonders."
